10 units, each with worked examples, a 10-mark practice set in CBSE question styles, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your board exam. Research check: this book follows NCERT Class 12 Physics Part 1, Chapter 1 (Electric Charges and Fields), for the CBSE 2026–27 session. The Physics theory paper is 70 marks in 3 hours, with 30 marks for practicals. Electrostatics (Chapters 1–2) and Current Electricity (Chapter 3) together carry 16 marks. Recent sample papers have 33 questions in five sections: A — 16 one-mark items (MCQs and assertion–reason); B — 5 two-mark; C — 7 three-mark; D — 2 four-mark case-based; E — 3 five-mark long answers. Topics follow the current syllabus: charge, Coulomb's law, superposition, continuous charge distributions, electric field and field lines, the electric dipole, electric flux, and Gauss's law for an infinite wire, an infinite plane sheet and a thin spherical shell.

Each unit ends with a 10-mark practice set in these styles. Constants: k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Every numerical answer was checked by computer. The marking points are our own, not the official CBSE marking scheme. Check the latest sample paper on cbseacademic.nic.in.

Unit 1 of 10: Electric Charge and Its Properties

Key ideas

  • Two kinds of charge: positive and negative; like charges repel, unlike attract.
  • Charging: by friction (electron transfer), conduction (contact) and induction (bringing a charged body near, earthing, then removing earth and the body).
  • Properties:
  1. Additivity: total charge is the algebraic sum — charges are scalars.
  2. Conservation: total charge of an isolated system stays constant; charge is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
  3. Quantisation: q = ±ne, where n is an integer and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Quantisation is not noticed at the macroscopic level because e is tiny (1 μC contains about 10¹³ electronic charges).
  • Conductors allow charges to move freely; insulators do not.

Worked examples

Example 1: Number of electrons in −1 C: n = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸.

Example 2: Can a body carry 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C? n = 2.4/1.6 = 1.5 — not an integer, so no.

Example 3: A glass rod rubbed with silk acquires +3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C. Electrons lost = 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2 × 10¹⁰; the silk gains −3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C (conservation).

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) Which charge is possible on a body? (a) 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (b) 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (c) 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (d) 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Answer: (c) (n = 2).
  2. (1 mark, assertion–reason) A: charge is quantised. R: charge on a body is always an integral multiple of e. Answer: (a).
  3. (2 marks) How many electrons must be removed from a neutral sphere to give it a charge of +8 μC? Answer: n = 8 × 10⁻⁶ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ (1) = 5 × 10¹³ (1).
  4. (3 marks) Explain how a metal sphere can be charged negatively by induction using a positively charged rod. Answer: bring the positive rod near; electrons are attracted to the near side (1); earth the sphere while the rod is near — electrons flow from earth to the sphere (1); remove the earth connection, then the rod; the sphere is left negatively charged (1).
  5. (3 marks) State three basic properties of electric charge with a one-line explanation of each. Answer: additivity — algebraic sum (1); conservation — total charge of an isolated system is constant (1); quantisation — q = ne (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Saying charge is a vector. 2. Forgetting the sign of e. 3. Removing the rod before breaking the earth connection in induction. 4. Non-integer n accepted as valid. 5. Power-of-ten errors with μC.

Quick recall

  1. Value of e? 2. Quantisation formula? 3. Is charge conserved in all processes? 4. Electrons in 1 C? 5. Charging without contact?

Answers: 1) 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 2) q = ne. 3) Yes. 4) 6.25 × 10¹⁸. 5) Induction.
